#### 4.2.3. Echocardiography for the Dilemma Vasopressors vs. Inotropes

Echocardiography provides a rapid, non-invasive means of defining the predominant hemodynamic phenotype and supporting individualized vasoactive therapy in shock. Rather than relying on isolated parameters, integration of ventricular function, forward flow, filling conditions, and preload responsiveness can help distinguish vasoplegia from myocardial dysfunction or hypovolemia [4,141]. A low-flow state with impaired LV contractility may support inotropic therapy, whereas preserved or hyperdynamic flow in the presence of persistent hypotension favors vasopressor treatment. Dynamic changes in LVOT VTI may additionally help determine whether further fluid administration is likely to increase stroke volume [155]. Assessment of RV function and afterload is particularly important because significant RV dysfunction may require avoidance of excessive vasoconstriction and adoption of RV-directed strategies [4,141]. Echocardiographic findings should therefore be interpreted as components of an evolving physiological profile rather than as fixed treatment thresholds. Serial reassessment after therapeutic interventions allows adjustment of fluids, vasopressors, and inotropes according to the changing hemodynamic state [4,141] ([Figure 3](#biomedicines-14-02157-f003)).

#### 4.2.4. Pulmonary Artery Catheterization (PAC) for the Dilemma: Vasopressors vs. Inotropes

Pulmonary artery catheterization (PAC) provides detailed invasive hemodynamic characterization and may be particularly useful in refractory or complex shock when the predominant mechanism remains uncertain despite initial assessment [14,183]. Simultaneous evaluation of cardiac output/index, filling pressures, SVR, pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR), and SvO2 can distinguish low-flow pump failure, vasoplegia, preload deficiency, congestion, and predominant RV dysfunction [184]. Low cardiac output with elevated filling pressures may support inotropic and decongestive strategies, whereas low SVR with preserved output favors vasopressor therapy. Conversely, low filling pressures may identify patients in whom cautious fluid administration remains appropriate [14,183]. Additional indices such as cardiac power output and PAPi can further characterize global pump performance and RV–pulmonary vascular interaction [14,183]. PAC-derived variables should be integrated with clinical and echocardiographic findings rather than interpreted as isolated therapeutic thresholds. Repeated hemodynamic assessment can subsequently guide adjustment of fluids, vasopressors, inotropes, and RV-directed therapy according to treatment response [14] ([Figure 4](#biomedicines-14-02157-f004)).

## 5. Integration into Multidisciplinary Shock Management

### 5.1. How Cardiology Contributes to ICU and Emergency Settings

The management of shock has progressively evolved into a multidisciplinary process in which cardiology plays a central role in both diagnosis and treatment. Beyond identifying primary cardiogenic shock, cardiologists are essential in recognizing secondary myocardial dysfunction in systemic conditions such as sepsis, where cardiac involvement is often dynamic and load-dependent. Differentiating between primary cardiac failure and mixed shock states is critical, as it directly influences therapeutic strategy and outcomes [8,185].

In contemporary intensive care and emergency settings, cardiology contributes to detailed hemodynamic profiling and treatment optimization. Through the integration of bedside echocardiography, advanced hemodynamic monitoring, and interpretation of complex cardiovascular interactions, cardiologists guide decisions regarding fluid resuscitation, vasoactive agents, and inotropic support [8]. In refractory or complex cases, they are instrumental in identifying candidates for mechanical circulatory support (MCS), including venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation and percutaneous ventricular assist devices, particularly when a cardiogenic component coexists or emerges during the course of illness [14,15,19,21].

### 5.2. Serial Echocardiographic Reassessment and Multidisciplinary Integration

The clinical value of echocardiography in shock extends beyond the initial identification of the predominant hemodynamic phenotype. Shock represents a dynamic process in which ventricular function, preload, afterload, pulmonary vascular loading, and systemic vascular tone may change substantially following fluid administration, vasoactive or inotropic therapy, mechanical ventilation, progression of the underlying disease, or definitive treatment of its cause [12,23]. Accordingly, echocardiographic findings should not be interpreted as a single diagnostic snapshot. Serial reassessment after major therapeutic interventions allows evaluation of whether the intended physiological response has occurred and whether the initial phenotype has persisted, resolved, or evolved into a mixed circulatory state [84,141,145].

### 5.3. Controversies, Limitations of Current Evidence, and Future Directions

Despite increasing recognition of cardiac dysfunction across shock states, important uncertainties limit the interpretation of the available literature. This is particularly evident in sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy, for which no universally accepted diagnostic definition exists [56]. Reported prevalence varies substantially according to the timing of assessment, loading conditions, and the echocardiographic parameter used. Left ventricular ejection fraction is highly afterload dependent and may therefore underestimate intrinsic myocardial dysfunction during profound vasoplegia, whereas global longitudinal strain may detect subtler abnormalities but remains dependent on image quality, technical expertise, and methodological standardization [23]. Similarly, right ventricular dysfunction in sepsis cannot always be attributed to intrinsic septic myocardial injury because mechanical ventilation, hypoxemia, hypercapnia, pulmonary vascular loading, and concomitant pulmonary disease may independently impair RV performance. Consequently, a single echocardiographic abnormality should not be interpreted as diagnostic of septic cardiomyopathy without consideration of loading conditions, competing diagnoses, and serial evolution [56].

Similar limitations apply to echocardiography-guided management. Contemporary critical-care guidance supports critical care ultrasonography for hemodynamic assessment in septic and cardiogenic shock and suggests its use for targeted volume management [186]. Nevertheless, the evidence is considerably stronger for echocardiography as a diagnostic and physiological monitoring tool than for individual echo-derived thresholds or phenotype-to-treatment algorithms as outcome-proven therapeutic strategies. Parameters such as IVC respiratory variation, LVOT VTI, E/e′, VExUS, and indices of RV–pulmonary arterial coupling are influenced by ventilation, rhythm, loading conditions, acquisition technique, and the clinical context. They should therefore be integrated rather than applied as isolated therapeutic triggers [186].

Therapeutic evidence is also uneven across shock phenotypes. Some interventions, such as norepinephrine as first-line vasopressor therapy in septic shock and immediate correction of reversible mechanical causes of obstructive shock, are supported by guideline-level evidence. In contrast, the optimal timing of additional vasopressors, selection of inotropic support according to specific echocardiographic phenotypes, advanced ultrasound-guided de-resuscitation strategies, and several RV-directed interventions remain supported predominantly by physiological rationale, observational evidence, or expert consensus. Accordingly, [Figure 2](#biomedicines-14-02157-f002), [Figure 3](#biomedicines-14-02157-f003) and [Figure 4](#biomedicines-14-02157-f004) should be interpreted as conceptual, physiology-based frameworks intended to organize hemodynamic assessment and clinical reasoning rather than as validated treatment algorithms or outcome-proven management pathways. Future prospective studies should evaluate standardized definitions of cardiac dysfunction, serial rather than single-time-point echocardiographic phenotyping, and whether integrated phenotype-guided treatment strategies improve patient-centered outcomes compared with conventional hemodynamic management. The recent literature continues to emphasize both the need for individualized septic-shock management and uncertainty surrounding several adjunctive vasoactive strategies [187].

## 6. Conclusions

Shock states arise from distinct pathophysiological mechanisms but may converge on impaired effective forward flow, altered ventricular loading, myocardial dysfunction in selected settings, and tissue hypoperfusion. Echocardiography provides a rapid means of characterizing ventricular function, loading conditions, forward flow, and reversible mechanical causes, while serial reassessment can identify evolving or mixed hemodynamic phenotypes. Integration of echocardiographic findings with clinical assessment and, when required, invasive hemodynamic data may support individualized resuscitation. However, individual echocardiographic or PAC-derived parameters should not be interpreted as standalone therapeutic targets, and several proposed phenotype-guided treatment strategies remain dependent on physiological rationale and observational evidence rather than outcome-proven algorithms.

**Figure 1.**
Simplified mechanisms of septic myocardial depression. Sepsis-induced myocardial dysfunction results from the interaction of multiple inflammatory, cellular, metabolic, and hemodynamic mechanisms rather than from global myocardial ischemia alone. Infection triggers innate immune activation through pathogen- and damage-associated molecular patterns, leading to cytokine release, nitric oxide overproduction, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired calcium handling, endothelial and microvascular injury, and myocardial edema. These processes collectively reduce myocardial contractility, impair relaxation, and contribute to variable left and right ventricular dysfunction. At the clinical level, the phenotype is dynamic and load-dependent, ranging from hyperdynamic circulation in the setting of vasoplegia to low-output states when intrinsic myocardial depression predominates. Importantly, septic myocardial depression is often reversible after control of infection and resolution of the systemic inflammatory response. Conceptual early integrated echocardiography framework for the evaluation and management of shock. Echocardiography is integrated concurrently with initial resuscitation and should not delay time-critical etiologic treatment. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS), including focused cardiac ultrasound (FoCUS) when cardiac assessment is required, may rapidly identify major obstructive or structural causes and characterize ventricular function, forward flow, loading conditions, and congestion. **Figure 3.**
Conceptual echocardiography-based framework for hemodynamic phenotyping and vasoactive management considerations in septic, hypovolemic, and obstructive shock. Focused echocardiography can help characterize the predominant shock phenotype and inform individualized fluid, vasoactive, and procedural management. In septic shock, assessment of filling, preload responsiveness, LVOT VTI, ventricular function, and right ventricular afterload may help distinguish fluid-responsive states, vasoplegia, myocardial dysfunction, and RV dysfunction. In hypovolemic shock, a small LV cavity, end-systolic obliteration, and low LVOT VTI may support fluid resuscitation when consistent with the clinical context, whereas venous congestion or elevated left-sided filling pressures may indicate limited fluid tolerance. In obstructive shock, echocardiography may identify tamponade or pulmonary embolism and facilitate urgent definitive management. Because these parameters are influenced by loading conditions and do not represent validated treatment thresholds, findings should be integrated with the clinical context and serially reassessed to guide individualized therapy and therapeutic response. **Figure 4.**
Conceptual PAC-informed hemodynamic framework for selected patients with refractory or complex shock. Pulmonary artery catheterization can provide detailed assessment of cardiac index, filling pressures, systemic and pulmonary vascular resistance, right-sided pressures, mixed venous oxygen saturation, and cardiac power. These variables may help characterize low-flow states, congestion, preload deficiency, vasoplegia, increased afterload, impaired systemic oxygen delivery, and predominant RV dysfunction. Low cardiac index with elevated PCWP may support consideration of inotropic and decongestive strategies, whereas low filling pressures may identify selected patients in whom cautious fluid administration remains appropriate. Low SVR with preserved or elevated cardiac index may support a vasodilatory phenotype, while high SVR with low cardiac index may indicate increased afterload. Low SvO2 or cardiac power may suggest inadequate systemic oxygen delivery, and a combination of low PAPi, elevated PVR, elevated RAP, and low cardiac output may support a predominantly RV-related phenotype. These variables should be integrated with clinical and echocardiographic findings and serially reassessed rather than interpreted as standalone treatment thresholds. (This figure represents a conceptual, physiology-based framework for clinical reasoning and serial reassessment; it has not been prospectively validated as a treatment algorithm and should not supersede established guideline-directed or etiology-specific management).
